what_its_for: Vutrisiran is used to treat a condition called hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR amyloidosis) in adults. This is a rare genetic disease where an abnormal protein called transthyretin (TTR) builds up in the body's tissues and organs, especially the nerves and heart, causing damage. This medicine works by reducing the amount of this harmful protein your body makes.
how_to_take: Vutrisiran is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), not into a vein. It is administered by a healthcare provider, such as a doctor or nurse, in a clinic or medical office. You should NOT inject this medicine yourself at home unless your healthcare provider has specifically trained you to do so. The injection is typically given in the belly (abdomen), thigh, or upper arm. Before each injection, you will receive two other medicines — an antihistamine and acetaminophen (Tylenol) — to help prevent injection site reactions.
dosing: The usual dose is 25 mg given as a single injection once every 3 months (4 times per year). Your healthcare provider will schedule your appointments. Do not miss your scheduled doses, as staying on schedule is important for this medicine to work properly.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your injection appointment, contact your healthcare provider as soon as possible to arrange a new appointment. Try to reschedule within a reasonable time. After rescheduling, your new every-3-month schedule will be based on the date of your next injection. Do not try to get two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Vutrisiran is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy — you do not need to store it at home in most cases. If you are given vials to bring to your appointment, keep them in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze the medicine. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. If taken out of the refrigerator, it can be kept at room temperature (up to 86°F / 30°C) for up to 6 months. Always check the expiration date before use.
what_to_avoid: There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you must strictly avoid while taking vutrisiran. However, you should: Tell ALL your doctors and pharmacists about every medicine, vitamin, herbal supplement, or over-the-counter drug you take, as drug interactions are possible. Avoid skipping your scheduled injection appointments. Do not start or stop any medications without checking with your healthcare provider first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your healthcare provider right away or seek emergency medical help if you experience any of the following: Severe allergic reaction symptoms such as hives, rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness after your injection. Signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, stomach pain, or unusual tiredness. Serious injection site reactions such as significant pain, redness, swelling, or skin changes that do not go away. New or worsening nerve symptoms such as numbness, tingling, weakness in your hands or feet, or balance problems. New or worsening heart symptoms such as shortness of breath, swelling in your legs or feet, or irregular heartbeat. Also let your doctor know right away if you become pregnant or are planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Vutrisiran starts reducing the amount of harmful TTR protein in your blood within about 1 month of your first injection. However, it may take several months before you notice an improvement in your symptoms such as less numbness, tingling, or weakness. Some patients may see stabilization of their condition rather than full reversal of symptoms. It is important to continue your scheduled injections every 3 months even if you feel well, because stopping treatment can allow the harmful protein levels to rise again.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Vutrisiran may harm an unborn baby. If you can become pregnant, use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: It is not known if vutrisiran passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Older adults (65 years and older): This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Dose adjustments are generally not needed for mild to moderate kidney or liver issues, but tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have. Children: Vutrisiran is not approved for use in patients under 18 years of age.
